abstract: The serotonin 2A receptor (5-HT2AR) is a target of drugs used to treat anxiety and mood disorders, yet whether endogenous 5-HT2AR signaling constrains or promotes anxiety, and how the 5-HT2AR affects cell populations linked to anxiety, is not fully resolved. Acute 5-HT2AR agonism is anxiolytic and acts through the activation of ventral hippocampal parvalbumin-expressing interneurons. Here we report that constitutive deletion of the 5-HT2AR in male and female BALB/c mice is associated with robust anxiety-like and repetitive behavior across multiple paradigms. Unbiased proteomic analysis of male knockout hippocampal tissue revealed substantially reduced levels of parvalbumin (PV), a proxy of their activity. Consistent with the intense metabolic demands of fast spiking interneurons, proteins supporting energy metabolism were also downregulated, including those related to oxidative phosphorylation and the electron transport chain, glycolysis and the tricarboxylic acid cycle, together with the cytoplasmic ribosome. In terms of how reduced 5-HT2AR signaling could lead to reduced PV expression, we examined key perineuronal net (PNN) components. The PNN constituents aggrecan and HAPLN1 were not significantly changed, whereas the link protein, HAPLN4 was substantially reduced. In a separate cohort, 7 days following a single dose of the selective 5-HT2AR agonist, 25CN-NBOH, many of the same energy metabolism proteins were shifted in the opposite direction. Together these findings indicate that constitutive loss of 5-HT2AR signaling is associated with coordinated reductions in parvalbumin and in the biosynthetic and bioenergetic machinery that supports fast-spiking activity, without a generalized loss of perineuronal net structural components.
